question.text:
Which of the following descriptions is true regarding APC-II (anterior-posterior compression) pelvic injuries as classified by Young and Burgess?
Answer Choices: (A) Pubic symphysis diastasis, intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, torn posterior sacroiliac ligaments (B) Pubic symphysis diastasis, torn posterior sacroiliac ligaments, intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament (C) Intact pubic symphysis, bilateral torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament (D) Pubic symphysis diastasis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, intact sacrotuberous ligament intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments (E) Pubic symphysis diastasis, intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments (F) Pubic symphysis diastasis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments (G) Pubic symphysis diastasis, bilateral torn sacroiliac ligaments, intact sacrotuberous ligament (H) Intact pubic symphysis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments (I) Pubic symphysis diastasis, unilateral torn anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, intact sacrotuberous ligament (J) Pubic symphysis diastasis with complete disruption of all pelvic ligaments

options.A: Pubic symphysis diastasis, intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, torn posterior sacroiliac ligaments
options.B: Pubic symphysis diastasis, torn posterior sacroiliac ligaments, intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament
options.C: Intact pubic symphysis, bilateral torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament
options.D: Pubic symphysis diastasis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, intact sacrotuberous ligament intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments
options.E: Pubic symphysis diastasis, intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments
options.F: Pubic symphysis diastasis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments
options.G: Pubic symphysis diastasis, bilateral torn sacroiliac ligaments, intact sacrotuberous ligament
options.H: Intact pubic symphysis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous ligament, intact posterior sacroiliac ligaments
options.I: Pubic symphysis diastasis, unilateral torn anterior and posterior sacroiliac ligaments, intact sacrotuberous ligament
options.J: Pubic symphysis diastasis with complete disruption of all pelvic ligaments

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: APC-II injuries involve disruption of the pubic symphysis and the sacroiliac ligaments. The key finding is the disruption of the sacrotuberous ligament, which is a hallmark of APC-II injuries. The anterior sacroiliac ligaments are typically intact.
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: Options B, C, D, E, F, G, H, I, and J are incorrect because they either misrepresent the location of the ligament tears or do not include the disruption of the sacrotuberous ligament. Option J is incorrect because it suggests complete disruption of all pelvic ligaments, which is not typical of APC-II injuries.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: APC-II injuries involve anterior-posterior compression, which typically results in pubic symphysis diastasis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments, and torn sacrotuberous ligament. The posterior sacroiliac ligaments remain intact in this classification.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Pubic symphysis diastasis with specific ligamentous injuries as described in option F
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: Other options either misidentify ligamentous injuries or include complete disruption of all ligaments, which is not characteristic of APC-II injuries

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: APC-II injuries, as per Young and Burgess classification, involve pubic symphysis diastasis with intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn posterior sacroiliac ligaments, and torn sacrotuberous ligament. This pattern reflects a specific biomechanical mechanism of anterior-posterior compression leading to distinct ligamentous disruptions.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: The defining features of APC-II are pubic symphysis diastasis, intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn posterior sacroiliac ligaments, and torn sacrotuberous ligament — exactly matching option A.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Other options like APC-I (intact pubic symphysis, torn anterior sacroiliac ligaments) or APC-III (complete ligament disruption) were considered but ruled out due to mismatch in ligamentous integrity and pubic symphysis status.

olmo3_7b.clinical_reasoning: APC-II pelvic injuries involve a diastasis of the pubic symphysis with specific ligamentous disruptions. According to Young and Burgess classification, this injury typically includes intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, a torn sacrotuberous ligament, and torn posterior sacroiliac ligaments. Option A matches this pattern, while other options either describe incomplete disruption, incorrect ligament integrity, or an impossible scenario (e.g., all ligaments disrupted in J).
olmo3_7b.critical_evidence: The classic description of APC-II injury is pubic symphysis diastasis with intact anterior sacroiliac ligaments, torn sacrotuberous and posterior sacroiliac ligaments.
olmo3_7b.differential_considered:
[
    "Options B, C, D, E, F, G, H, and I incorrectly state the integrity of at least one of the key pelvic ligaments as intact when the standard description requires them to be torn in APC-II. Option J describes a complete disruption of all ligaments, which is more severe than the standard APC-II injury.
